title: Haiti Environmental Crisis
description: Haiti's environmental crisis is not a single disaster but a prolonged struggle in which deforestation, pollution, climate vulnerability, and weak governance reinforce one another. For decades, reliance on charcoal and firewood has driven severe forest loss, stripping hillsides of protection and making watersheds far more vulnerable to floods and landslides. Rapid urbanization has outpaced public services, while soil erosion, overfishing, and climate shocks translate into economic destruction and food insecurity. Haiti is responsible for a negligible share of global emissions, yet pays an outsized price—trapped in a cycle where poverty, environmental collapse, and political instability feed one another.

dr_elena.name: Dr. Elena
dr_elena.role: Senior Economist, Monetary Policy & Financial Stability Division
dr_elena.personality: Analytical, cautious, sensitive to systemic fragility
dr_elena.motivation: Identify leverage points where economic and environmental policy can reinforce each other
dr_elena.opening_scene: Dr. Elena arrives in Port-au-Prince as an international economic advisor. The hillsides are bare — stripped by years of charcoal dependency. Below, the city struggles under flooding and waste. She opens her briefing notes: the economy, the environment, and public order are all in crisis simultaneously. She has five decisions to make.

questions.text: Mudslides tear through deforested land. A local official says: "The hills used to hold. Now they collapse." A community leader adds: "We rebuild every year yet lose everything again." How do you build resilience against worsening natural disasters?
questions.fun_fact: Only about 1% of Haiti's original forest cover remains, leaving hillsides exposed to erosion and catastrophic flooding during tropical storms.

options.text: Focus on emergency disaster relief (food, shelters, short-term aid).
options.feedback: Aid flows in. Families survive—but return to the same exposed land. A mother says: "We rebuild… again."

options.text: Invest in basic infrastructure (drainage, flood barriers in cities).
options.feedback: Cities improve. But rural migrants flood into Port-au-Prince, worsening overcrowding.

options.text: Launch reforestation + watershed restoration programs.
options.feedback: Hills slowly recover. Farmers wait years for results. Some abandon land.

options.text: Combine infrastructure, reforestation, and community-led resilience planning.
options.feedback: Communities begin adapting. Progress is uneven—but for the first time, prevention exists.

questions.text: A farmer says: "If I don't cut trees, my family doesn't eat." How do you address charcoal-driven deforestation?
questions.fun_fact: An estimated 63% of Haiti's natural forest land recorded in 2002 remains—tree felling for charcoal has become a means of survival for many families.

options.text: Ban tree cutting and enforce penalties.
options.feedback: Forest loss slows. Protests rise. Illegal cutting increases.

options.text: Educate communities on environmental damage.
options.feedback: Awareness grows—but trees continue to fall.

options.text: Subsidize alternative fuels (gas, solar cooking).
options.feedback: Some transition away from charcoal. Others cannot afford the shift.

options.text: Combine enforcement, alternative energy, and income programs.
options.feedback: Gradual transition begins. Forest loss slows while livelihoods stabilize.

questions.text: A fisherman says: "The fish are gone. So we go farther… or we go hungry." How do you address overfishing and food insecurity?
questions.fun_fact: Agriculture employs 66% of Haiti's population; deep poverty perpetuated by climate change drives overfishing in a vicious cycle for fishing families.

options.text: Allow open fishing to preserve livelihoods.
options.feedback: Short-term survival improves. Fish stocks collapse rapidly.

options.text: Set fishing limits and seasonal bans.
options.feedback: Stocks recover slowly. Hunger rises in fishing communities.

options.text: Provide food aid + alternative employment programs.
options.feedback: Food security improves—but economic independence weakens.

options.text: Combine regulation, aquaculture investment, and job creation.
options.feedback: Fishing pressure decreases. New industries emerge—slow but stabilizing.

questions.text: Youth protesters in Port-au-Prince say: "No jobs. No food. No future." How do you respond to rising unrest?
questions.fun_fact: Flooding and subsequent droughts push some individuals into the desperation of violence; as youth struggle with food and climate insecurity, many are swept up by gang affiliation.

options.text: Deploy security forces to restore order.
options.feedback: Protests quiet—but tensions deepen. Violence simmers.

options.text: Provide emergency food + cash relief.
options.feedback: Immediate calm. However, crisis returns once aid fades.

options.text: Launch youth employment + public works programs.
options.feedback: Hope rises slowly. Some unrest continues.

options.text: Combine security restraint, aid, and long-term economic programs.
options.feedback: Stability improves gradually. Trust rebuilds—fragile but real.

questions.text: An advisor says: "The crisis isn't ending. It's evolving." What long-term strategy do you pursue?
questions.fun_fact: Haiti is one of the most vulnerable countries to climate change impacts, given its acute poverty, rapid population growth, and unplanned urbanization.

options.text: Focus on economic growth first, environment later.
options.feedback: Growth improves briefly. Environmental collapse accelerates.

options.text: Incremental environmental reforms.
options.feedback: Some progress. Vulnerabilities remain.

options.text: Aggressive climate adaptation policies.
options.feedback: Resilience improves. Economic strain increases.

options.text: Integrated climate + economic transformation strategy.
options.feedback: Gradual transformation. Haiti becomes more adaptive—though challenges persist.

result_bands.title: Scenario 1: Fragile / Crisis Deepens
result_bands.summary: Reactive measures provide temporary relief but fail to break the cycle. Deforestation accelerates, food insecurity worsens, and unrest grows. The crisis compounds faster than institutions can respond.
simple_summary: No real progress on root causes

result_bands.title: Scenario 2: Strained but Holding
result_bands.summary: Emergency interventions prevent immediate collapse, but structural vulnerabilities persist. Some communities stabilize while others remain exposed. Dependence on external aid continues.

result_bands.title: Scenario 3: Gradual Recovery
result_bands.summary: Targeted policies slow environmental degradation and reduce food insecurity. Livelihoods begin to stabilize, and trust in institutions cautiously recovers. Progress is real but fragile.

result_bands.title: Scenario 4: Adaptive Resilience
result_bands.summary: Integrated strategies address root causes across environment, economy, and governance simultaneously. Communities become more resilient, forest cover begins to return, and new livelihoods emerge.
